I used to track one metric: velocity.

It felt like the right move. Stakeholders loved it. "The team delivered 42 points last sprint!" Everyone nodded.

Then at Adidas, I joined a team with a beautiful velocity — and a 60% defect escape rate. Fast delivery. Into production. Broken.

That's when I realised velocity only tells you how fast you ran. Not whether you ran in the right direction. Not whether what you built actually worked.

I started tracking three things instead:

Velocity — still useful, but only as one signal, not the headline.

Cycle time — how long does it take a ticket to go from "In Progress" to "Done"? This exposes hidden bottlenecks nobody talks about in standup.

Defect escape rate — how many bugs are reaching production? This tells you about your team's quality culture, not just their speed.

When all three move together — velocity steady, cycle time shrinking, defect rate dropping — your team is genuinely improving. When only velocity climbs? Something is being hidden.

These three metrics changed how I coach teams. Not by adding pressure, but by making the invisible visible.

Sprint after sprint, we over-committed. Every time.

I brought the data to the next planning session. No commentary. Just the chart.

The room went quiet.

We made one change: we stopped planning 100% capacity. We reserved a buffer — roughly 30% — for unplanned work. Then we planned the rest with realistic story estimates based on historical throughput, not gut feel.

First sprint with the new approach: we delivered 94% of what we committed.

The team didn't change. The plan changed. Because the data finally told us the truth about our sprints.

How many stories are sitting in "In Progress" for more than 3 days? That's your real risk indicator.

How many stories have zero activity in the last 48 hours? Silent tasks are stuck tasks.

Are stories moving forward or just being updated to look like they are?

A burndown chart shows you story points. It doesn't show you reality. The Scrum Master's job is to see through the number and into the actual work.

I asked 8 Scrum Masters to define cycle time. I got 8 different answers.

At ABB, when I first started tracking flow metrics, I assumed cycle time and lead time were the same thing. A lot of people do.

They are not — and confusing them will send you after the wrong problem.

Lead time is the full clock: from the moment a stakeholder makes a request, to the moment it is delivered. This is the experience from the outside.

Cycle time is the active work clock: from when a developer picks up a ticket, to when it is done. This is the experience from the inside.

When I mapped both for our team at ABB, I found something striking: our cycle time was 2.3 days. Our lead time was 11 days. The actual work was fast. The waiting was the problem.

Stories sat in the backlog for over a week before anyone touched them. Once started, they moved quickly. The bottleneck was not the team — it was the intake process and prioritisation.

If I had only looked at cycle time, I would have optimised the wrong thing. Lead time showed me where the real waste was hiding.

Does your team track both? Which one reveals the bigger problem for you?

High defect rates are never just a QA problem.

At Adidas, I was brought in to help stabilise a delivery team that was shipping broken features into UAT almost every sprint. The default assumption was that QA needed more resources.

I pulled three months of defect data and categorised every bug by root cause.

What I found had nothing to do with testing capacity.

38% of bugs came from requirements that were never properly clarified. Developers had made assumptions — reasonable ones — but nobody had verified them with the Product Owner before build started.

29% came from last-minute scope changes that were added verbally in standup without updating acceptance criteria.

Only 18% were genuine technical defects.

The defect rate wasn't a testing problem. It was a communication problem. Stories were starting with too many open questions, and the cracks showed up in UAT.

We introduced a simple Definition of Ready — no story enters a sprint without clear acceptance criteria, edge cases documented, and a 15-minute refinement sign-off. Within two sprints, defect rates dropped by 35%.

Numbers don't just measure quality. They reveal how a team communicates.

At ABB Switzerland, we were mid-sprint on a high-visibility release. The energy in the team was confident — "we've got this." But I had started tracking daily progress rates, and by Wednesday morning, the numbers told a different story.

We had completed 8 out of 34 story points in 3 days. At that pace, we would finish roughly 60% of the sprint. And three of the remaining stories hadn't been touched at all.

I raised it in standup. "Based on our current throughput, we're on track to deliver about 22 points by Friday."

The team pushed back. "We'll pick up speed in the second week." "The big stories are almost done." Classic optimism bias — I've been there myself.

I didn't argue. I put the projected completion rate on a shared doc and updated it daily.

By day 7, the numbers were undeniable. We course-corrected: descoped two lower-priority stories, escalated one external dependency that had been sitting unanswered for four days, and restructured the final two days.

We delivered 28 out of 34 points. Not perfect — but far better than the 14 we were headed for without intervention.

Data doesn't save sprints. Acting on data early does.

Velocity tells you how fast you ran. It doesn't tell you if you ran in the right direction.

At Verizon, I inherited a team that had been hitting their velocity target for six straight sprints. Leadership was happy. Numbers looked great.

Then the Product Owner ran a quarterly business review and found that 30% of features delivered in those six sprints had zero adoption. Users weren't using them. Some had never been requested by anyone who actually used the product.

The team was fast. But fast at building the wrong things.

Velocity had become a target rather than a tool. Stories were being split to inflate points. Low-complexity tasks were being picked first to hit the number. High-value, high-complexity work was consistently deferred.

I introduced two additional metrics alongside velocity: customer adoption rate for delivered features, and business value score — a simple 1–5 rating agreed with the Product Owner before each sprint.

Over time, velocity actually dropped slightly — because we stopped gaming it. But delivery of real business value went up. And the quarterly review six months later looked very different.

Metrics shape behaviour. Track the wrong ones and you get the wrong results, delivered very efficiently.
